_comment: Edit this file to add gallery items. Each item: id, book, category (photography|painting|literature|object), title, date, source, url (page URL), image_url (direct .jpg/.png for tag), credit, description, location_ref (POI id or empty). Notes: Yasaka Pagoda item is CC-BY 2.0 (requires attribution). Osaka 1930s scans are low-resolution (~400–530px). Literature items are document pages — use 'url' to link out, no image_url.

items.title: Marunouchi 'London Street', looking toward the Imperial Palace
items.description: Babasaki Street's row of Western brick blocks nicknamed 'London Street.' The Marunouchi business district is the heart of corporate Tokyo where the targets of Isao's assassination plot are headquartered.

items.title: Marunouchi after the Great Kantō Earthquake
items.credit: Unknown / public domain — scan from Mainichi 'Shōwa History Vol. 4'
items.description: Marunouchi in the immediate aftermath of the 1923 earthquake. The Marunouchi Building (Marubiru) opened the same year; the district rebuilds into the financial center targeted in Runaway Horses a decade later.

items.title: Tokyo Station Marunouchi Building, entrance hall
items.description: The grand red-brick Tokyo Station at the foot of Marunouchi, completed 1914 — the gateway to the capital's financial district in the 1932 world of Runaway Horses.

items.title: The Ginza, looking north — 'the most important thoroughfare in Tokyo'
items.credit: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division — no known restrictions
items.description: An electrified-streetcar view of the Ginza in late-Meiji Tokyo, capturing the modernizing capital that frames the aristocratic world of Spring Snow.

items.title: Crowded Tokyo street near the train station (Admiral Tōgō celebration)
items.credit: Underwood & Underwood / Library of Congress — public domain
items.description: A dense Meiji Tokyo street scene during a victory celebration, evoking the bustling capital outside the secluded aristocratic estates of Spring Snow.

items.title: Gakushūin (Peers' School) girls' division at Yasukuni Shrine
items.description: Gakushūin, the Peers' School, is where Kiyoaki and Honda study together in Spring Snow. Photo is later than the novel's setting; the institution and its ethos are the same.

items.title: Nara, temple district (Plate 28, 'Sights and Scenes in Fair Japan')
items.description: A 1914 collotype of Nara by master photographer Kazumasa Ogawa, contemporaneous with Spring Snow. Nara and the fictional Gesshūji convent in its hills form the novel's devastating final movement.

items.title: Five-story pagoda and Sarusawa Pond, Nara
items.credit: New York Public Library — public domain
items.description: Kōfukuji's five-story pagoda reflected in Sarusawa Pond — the classic Nara vista.

items.title: Hōkan-ji Yasaka Pagoda, Higashiyama, Kyoto (hand-coloured lantern slide)
items.description: The Yasaka Pagoda in Kyoto's Higashiyama district, evoking the temple atmosphere near Nanzenji referenced in Spring Snow's Kyoto scenes. Note: CC-BY license, attribution required.

items.title: Tenjuan temple garden, Nanzenji, Kyoto
items.description: A raked garden at Nanzenji, the Kyoto temple complex near the settings of Kiyoaki and Satoko's clandestine meetings in Spring Snow.

items.title: Ise Shrine — Plate 22, 'Sights and Scenes in Fair Japan' (Kazumasa Ogawa)
items.description: A 1914 collotype capturing the cypress architecture of Ise Jingū — the shrine's forest and river that intensify Isao's conviction of divine mission in Runaway Horses.

items.title: Dōtonbori, Osaka, in the 1930s
items.credit: Unknown / public domain — from Asahi Shimbun 'Glimpses of Nippon'
items.description: Osaka's Dōtonbori entertainment district in the early Shōwa years — the bustling urban Osaka contemporaneous with the 1932 setting of Runaway Horses. Low-resolution scan.

items.title: Shinsaibashi-suji, Osaka, in the 1930s
items.credit: Unknown / public domain — from Asahi Shimbun 'Glimpses of Nippon'
items.description: The Shinsaibashi shopping street in 1930s Osaka. Low-resolution scan.

items.title: Japanese sailors practising kendo fencing aboard ship
items.credit: Bain News Service / Library of Congress — no known restrictions
items.description: Kendo practice in bōgu armor, the martial discipline embodied by Isao Iinuma and his dojo comrades in Runaway Horses.

items.title: Two boys in kendo dress
items.description: Young kendoka in full uniform, evoking the youthful martial idealism of Isao and his comrades in Runaway Horses.

items.title: Members of the Takanawa Fencing School ('The Fighting Man of Japan')
items.credit: Public domain — from 'The Fighting Man of Japan'
items.description: A formal portrait of a Tokyo kendo school's members, directly evoking the dojo brotherhood at the center of Runaway Horses.

items.title: Suruga Miho no Matsubara — Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, no. 24
items.credit: Utagawa Hiroshige, 1858 / Library of Congress — public domain
items.description: Hiroshige's woodblock print of the Miho pine grove on Suruga Bay with Mount Fuji beyond, from his Thirty-six Views series.

items.title: Emperor Meiji Worshipping at Ise Grand Shrine (ukiyo-e)
items.description: The young Emperor Meiji's procession to Ise, fusing imperial reverence and Shinto pilgrimage — the ideology that drives the protagonists of Runaway Horses.

items.title: Genji Monogatari Emaki — 'Takekawa' (Bamboo River) chapter
items.credit: Heian court painters, c. 1130 (Tokugawa Art Museum) / public domain
items.description: A section of the 12th-century National Treasure Genji Monogatari Emaki. The Heian courtly aesthetic of the Tale of Genji underlies the elegiac mood of Spring Snow.

items.title: Genji Monogatari Emaki — 'Hashihime' (Bridge Princess) chapter
items.credit: Heian court painters, c. 1130 (Tokugawa Art Museum) / public domain
items.description: Courtly interiors and jūnihitoe robes from the earliest extant Genji handscroll — the classical world that informs Kiyoaki and Satoko's refined sensibility.

items.title: Genji Monogatari Emaki — 'Yadorigi' (Mistletoe) chapter
items.credit: Heian court painters, c. 1130 (Tokugawa Art Museum) / public domain
items.description: High-resolution section of the National Treasure Genji emaki — the touchstone of Heian aristocratic visual culture echoed throughout Spring Snow.

items.title: Uemura Shōen — 'Flower Basket' (Hanagatami)
items.description: Nihonga painting by Uemura Shōen, 1915. A woman in formal dress carries a flower basket. Shōen was one of the leading painters of the Taishō era, known for her portraits of women in classical Japanese settings.

items.title: Uemura Shōen — 'Firefly' (Hotaru)
items.description: Nihonga painting by Uemura Shōen, 1913. A woman in summer dress sits beneath a hanging mosquito net in the warm dusk, holding a fan. One of Shōen's celebrated series of women in quiet domestic interiors.

items.title: The Shinpūren Rebellion (Kumamoto Uprising)
items.description: Yoshitoshi's 1876 print of the Shinpūren (Divine Wind League) Rebellion in Kumamoto — the historical sword-bearing samurai uprising against Westernization that Isao reveres and consciously emulates in Runaway Horses.

items.title: Repression of the Shinpūren Rebellion
items.description: A contemporary painting depicting the suppression of the Shinpūren uprising — the doomed ultranationalist revolt whose tragic self-sacrifice is the explicit model for Runaway Horses.

items.title: Shinpūren no ran — Attack on Major General Taneda Masaaki
items.description: A nishikie depicting the rebels' night attack during the Shinpūren Rebellion — the historical event the dojo youths study in the 'League of the Divine Wind' chronicle within Runaway Horses.

items.title: Klong (canal), native houses, Bangkok
items.description: Bangkok's network of klongs (canals) gave the city its old nickname 'Venice of the East.' This watery, lush cityscape is the backdrop for Honda's diplomatic stay in The Temple of Dawn.

items.title: Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, on the Chao Phraya River
items.description: The towering porcelain-encrusted prang of Wat Arun rises from the riverbank — the temple that gives the third novel its title, and the site of Honda's first encounter with Princess Ying Chan.

items.title: Wat Benchamabophit, the Marble Temple, Bangkok
items.description: Built of gleaming Carrara marble under King Chulalongkorn, this is one of Bangkok's most striking modern temples and part of the royal temple landscape Honda moves through during his stay.

items.title: Wat Pho, Temple of the Reclining Buddha, Bangkok
items.description: One of Bangkok's oldest and largest temple complexes, home to the immense gold-leafed reclining Buddha — emblematic of the ornate Thai Buddhist architecture that fascinates and unsettles Honda.

items.title: The Grand Palace, Bangkok
items.description: The glittering complex of spires and gilded roofs that housed the Thai royal family — the setting for Honda's audience with the young Princess Ying Chan and her royal cousins.

items.title: Life on the Klongs (canals) of Bangkok
items.description: Laden cargo boats and wooden houses lining a Bangkok canal. The city's network of klongs functioned as streets, markets, and thoroughfares — Bangkok earned the name 'Venice of the East' from Western visitors who found the same watery, mercantile logic at work.

items.title: Khlong Somdet, Bangkok
items.description: A 1907 photograph of Khlong Somdet — one of Bangkok's main commercial canals, lined with houses on stilts and boat traffic. The canal system was the primary means of transport and trade in the city well into the twentieth century.

items.title: Morning at a jungle river, Southeast Asia
items.description: Dense tropical riverine jungle of the kind that surrounds Bangkok and the Thai countryside — the lush, humid, overgrown world so different from the austere landscapes of the earlier volumes.

items.title: Benares architecture beside the Ganges
items.description: The crowded stone steps of Benares descending into the Ganges, where pilgrims bathe and the dead are cremated in full view — the vision of cyclical life and death that anchors Honda's journey to India.

items.title: Wat Phra Kaew — Temple of the Emerald Buddha
items.description: Thailand's most sacred site, within the Grand Palace compound. Its inner gallery walls bear 178 panels of Ramakien murals (the Thai Ramayana). Honda passes through this world as a lawyer-tourist, unaware that Ying Chan's lineage connects to the Chakri dynasty who built it.

items.title: Ramakien Murals, Grand Palace gallery
items.description: One panel from the 178-panel Ramakien gallery lining the cloister of Wat Phra Kaew. The Ramakien is the Thai adaptation of the Hindu Ramayana — the mythological world that underpins the royal culture Honda enters in Bangkok.

items.title: Garuda — National Emblem of Thailand
items.description: The Garuda (Khrut) — mythological bird-vehicle of Vishnu in Hindu cosmology and the national emblem of Thailand. Honda sees it on temple pediments, royal seals, and government buildings throughout Bangkok. A constant reminder that the Thai state is a Hindu-Buddhist cosmological order, not a Western nation-state.

items.title: Kali — Kalighat Painting, Calcutta
items.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art / CC0 public domain
items.description: A Kalighat patachitra from Calcutta — the bold, confrontational folk-painting tradition of Bengal. Kali, goddess of death and time, presides over the Hindu religious world Honda encounters in Calcutta and Benares: death not as tragedy but as cosmic mechanism.

items.title: Ajanta Caves — Buddhist Cave Murals
items.description: The cave temples of Ajanta in Maharashtra, carved between the 2nd century BCE and 5th century CE, bear extraordinary murals of Jataka tales and Bodhisattvas. Honda's visit here — the site where accumulated philosophical reading crystallises into felt knowledge — is one of the novel's pivotal scenes.

items.title: Manikarnika Ghat (The Burning Ghat), Varanasi
items.description: The principal cremation ground of Varanasi, burning continuously day and night. Honda watching bodies reduced to ash here is one of The Temple of Dawn's most important scenes — death as quotidian fact rather than sacred exception, and the scene where Buddhist theory meets concrete physical reality.

items.title: Imperial Hotel, Tokyo — Frank Lloyd Wright building
items.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's Imperial Hotel — its distinctive Mayan-inflected Oya-stone facade survived the 1923 earthquake and stood until 1968. Honda and Ying Chan dine here explicitly in the novel, in the novel's 1952 section: a monument to a Japan that survived catastrophe and remade itself under Western aesthetic influence.

items.title: Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha, Fujinomiya
items.description: The main sanctuary of Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha in Fujinomiya — the head shrine of all Sengen shrines, sitting at the base of Mount Fuji in old cedar forest. Honda's group visits 'the shrine of Mount Fuji' in the novel. Vermilion shrine buildings, the mountain directly above, the sacred cedar dark around them.

items.title: Hokusai — Reflection in Lake at Misaka, Kai Province
items.source: Wikimedia Commons (The Metropolitan Museum of Art)
items.credit: Katsushika Hokusai, c. 1830–32 / The Met Open Access — CC0
items.description: Fuji inverted in a lake at Misaka — from Hokusai's Thirty-six Views series. The reflected mountain, indistinguishable from the real one, resonates with the novel's central question: which of the lives Honda has witnessed is the reflection, and which the original?

items.title: View toward Mount Fuji
items.description: The view of Fuji from the Gotemba plateau, where Honda builds the villa that becomes the stage for his obsessive watching of Ying Chan — and later, the central setting of The Decay of the Angel.

items.title: Mahāmayūrī Vidyārājñī Sūtra (Peacock Gold Sutra)
items.description: A protective Mahayana text centred on Mahāmayūrī — the Great Peacock Wisdom Queen, four-armed, seated on a peacock. Honda reads it as part of his investigation into karmic protection and reincarnation. The sutra's central parable: a golden peacock king who loses his protection through forgetfulness and is captured by hunters — an allegory for Honda's own lapse into voyeurism.

items.title: Laws of Manu — Manusmṛti
items.description: The foundational Sanskrit text of Hindu dharma — caste, karma, cosmology, and the ordering of lives across rebirths. Honda works through it alongside Buddhist texts to map the Hindu theory of transmigration against the Theravāda framework he encountered in Thailand. The two systems converge on the fact of rebirth but diverge sharply on whether anything substantial survives the crossing.

items.title: The Questions of King Milinda — Milindapañha
items.description: A Theravāda text recording exchanges between the Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the monk Nāgasena on whether a continuous self transmigrates or only a stream of moments. The philosophical core of Honda's obsession. Nāgasena's lamp-flame analogy — one flame lighting another, neither identical nor wholly separate — is the closest the tradition comes to answering him.

items.title: The City of the Sun — Tommaso Campanella
items.description: A perfect city organised around solar worship, communal rational order, and the elimination of private desire — written by Campanella while imprisoned by the Inquisition. Honda reads it as a counterpoint to everything his life has become: where Campanella's citizens are arranged in concentric circles of pure reason, Honda is crouched at a peephole in the wall of his own villa in Minami Daira.

items.title: Almsgiving of St. Rocco — Annibale Carracci
items.description: St. Roch distributes coins to plague victims on the steps below him — the saint present in the suffering, touching it. Honda references this painting as an image of charity he cannot enact: he watches, observes, and occasionally distributes money, but never enters the suffering he surveys. The painting is the indictment.

items.title: Album of Illustrations for the Tale of Genji (hakubyō ink album)
items.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0 public domain — full download available
items.description: A 17th-century accordion album illustrating the Tale of Genji in the delicate 'white drawing' (hakubyō) style. Downloadable in full from the Internet Archive.

items.title: The Small Mirror of Genji (illustrated Edo digest of the Tale of Genji)
items.credit: Library of Congress — public domain, full PDF available
items.description: A brightly illustrated 17th-century digest of the Tale of Genji, fully digitized as PDF. Provides classical Genji manuscript pages connecting to the Heian world evoked in Spring Snow.

items.title: Genji Monogatari (Saga-bon style edition, vol. 49)
items.description: A digitized Edo-period printed edition of the Tale of Genji from the Smithsonian's open-access collection — a primary-source manifestation of the classical text underpinning Spring Snow.
